articles.title: Nvidia will investigate CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with possible Chinese spy
articles.summary: In a memo to the company, Huang admitted that he had an affair.
articles.content:
Nvidia’s board of directors
announced
Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation following reports that
CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation
.
Nvidia also
published a message
that Huang sent to the company admitting that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed (though he didn’t mention her by name). A memo circulating among U.S. policymakers earlier this year
claimed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security
to spy on Nvidia’s CEO.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Huang added that he’d “fallen short” of his responsibility to the company.
“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” he said.
As
the AI race between the United States and China heats up
, chips, especially Nvidia’s chips, have been
a major focus
. Huang also seems to have
a close relationship with President Donald Trump
, who’s been a cheerleader of the AI (
or “superintelligence”
) industry.
In its announcement, Nvidia’s board said that it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or company secrets were compromised. It also said that Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” and that the board has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”
The investigation will be conducted by independent directors working with outside legal counsel.
In response to earlier reports about the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, Nvidia had said that the pair’s interactions were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with customers.
Other companies involved in the AI boom have
warned employees to be wary of possible spies
, including those offering sex or romance.

Terrence O'Brien
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.
Bloomberg’s
Mark Gurman says CEO John Ternus is pressuring AI czar Craig Federighi to
accelerate the Siri roadmap
and deliver a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI’s Dots or Meta’s Muse. While Federighi has delivered a functional version of Siri AI on an incredibly short timeline, the company has no illusions that it’s keeping pace with its rivals.
Two significant improvements are expected to be made to Siri in the coming months. One will give the assistant fine-grained control over Apple’s first-party apps, allowing it to do things like rotate and crop images in Photos and organize Safari tabs. Those capabilities are expected to land with iOS 27.3. The bigger change, integration with third-party apps, is likely to land later, in the Spring, according to Gurman. That would let Siri place an order through Grubhub or book a dinner reservation through OpenTable, for example.
But that’s just the start. Apple is expected to push Siri to become more agentic and enable features that will allow it to perform ongoing tasks, not just one-offs. Gurman says:
Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step. Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year — not that it has much of a choice, given current consumer and market demands.

Terrence O'Brien
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.
Suno is facing yet another
pair of lawsuits
. A group of rights holders of Elvis Presley’s music and the publisher of some of Eminem‘s biggest records are suing the AI music company, claiming it illegally generates music and lyrics that mimic those artists. The lawyers in the Presley suit claim that Suno has violated Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security (ELVIS) Act, which makes it illegal for an AI company to clone a singer’s voice.
In the suit, lawyers representing Presley’s rights holders argue that “Suno has mechanically encoded itself with artists’ identities, hard-work, creativity, and time, and harnessed them all for a consistent conveyor belt of
cold hard cash.“ These suits closely mirror one filed by Jason Isbell and others in September, which claimed Suno created imitations of the plaintiffs but did not claim copyright infringement directly.
Later in the
complaint
, the lawyers write that “Suno’s ravenous race to the bottom aims to make human creativity obsolete, coldly replicating without a license in seconds what takes years to learn, struggle with, maintain, and endlessly attempt to make better and perfect.”
Suno spokesperson Cat McCormack told The Verge that, “Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone’s name or likeness, and we prohibit any unauthorized use of an artist’s work. To protect against this, we do not allow prompts for specific artists’ names and songs and work with third-party providers to screen uploaded audio files and lyrics for potential misuse. We are always working to strengthen our guardrails and we will continue to add new safeguards that protect artists and our users.”
This adds to the pile of lawsuits Suno is currently facing from
Sony, UMG
, Isbell,
Reservoir Media
, and more.

Karpathy says he let Claude Code handle nearly all the work, from data analysis to server setup. His only manual steps were a Google Cloud API key, a rented server, and buying the domain. Projects that used to take weeks can now be done in a few hours, Karpathy says.

articles.title: The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate
articles.summary:
Consciousness researchers Anil Seth, Ned Block, and Giulio Tononi argue in a Nature commentary that today's AI systems aren't conscious and won't become so on silicon hardware. They consider the assumption that consciousness depends on computation alone "fatally flawed" and warn against granting rights to AI systems.
The article The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate appeared first on The Decoder.
articles.content:
Title: The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/the-brain-as-computer-metaphor-shaped-modern-ai-but-may-be-misleading-the-consciousness-debate/

Published Time: 2026-11-08T13:49:21+00:00

Markdown Content:
In their [commentary for Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03313-7), the authors also point to a study Anthropic published this year. The company reported [internal processing patterns in Claude](https://the-decoder.com/claudes-hidden-inner-monologue-is-now-readable-thanks-to-anthropics-new-jacobian-lens/) that resemble properties of consciously accessible information processing. Anthropic doesn't see this as evidence of subjective experience.

## The Butlin report agrees on today but leaves tomorrow open

To understand the scope of the commentary, it helps to look at the [report "Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08708) by Patrick Butlin, Robert Long, and 17 other experts, including AI researcher Yoshua Bengio. The team drew on leading neuroscientific theories about how consciousness arises in the human brain and derived [a kind of checklist](https://the-decoder.com/researchers-identify-potential-indicators-of-consciousness-in-ai-systems/) with 14 indicators. The more of these an AI system meets, the stronger the case that it could be conscious.

The researchers then evaluated several current systems, including large language models like GPT-4. The report concludes that none of the systems examined is a strong candidate for consciousness. On that point, it aligns with Seth, Block, and Tononi. For language models, Butlin and colleagues found only weak signs that the models meet the indicators of one of the most prominent consciousness theories at all. At the same time, the report sees no obvious technical barriers to [building future AI systems that meet more indicators](https://the-decoder.com/why-chatgpt-isnt-conscious-but-future-ai-systems-might-be/). Whether such systems would actually be conscious remains open. The authors specifically softened an earlier, stronger formulation on this point.

There's also a foundational assumption. The team assumed that consciousness depends solely on the type of information processing, not on whether it happens in nerve cells or computer chips. Experts call this computational functionalism. The authors adopted this assumption explicitly "for pragmatic reasons" because it's what makes it possible to examine AI systems for consciousness in the first place. The report itself acknowledged that its indicators would no longer be reliable if consciousness is tied to properties of living organisms. It cited Anil Seth, among others, as a proponent of that opposing view. That's where the Nature commentary picks up.

## Intelligence and consciousness aren't the same thing

The authors argue that consciousness is what disappears during dreamless sleep or general anesthesia and returns when you wake up or dream. Drawing on philosopher Thomas Nagel, they describe it this way: "Conscious experiences feel like something." Intelligence, by contrast, means carrying out functions. One doesn't follow from the other.

Their evidence is the human cerebellum. It contains nearly four-fifths of all neurons in the brain and plans movements with precision, speed, and the ability to learn. None of this happens consciously. If the cerebellum is missing or removed, consciousness isn't directly affected, the authors say.

The authors trace the confusion between intelligence and consciousness to two psychological tendencies. People see the world through their own lens and [attribute human qualities to things](https://the-decoder.com/google-deepmind-researchers-call-for-limits-on-ai-that-mimics-humans/). Language has long been considered something uniquely human. But language models are trained on vast amounts of human text that often deals with thoughts and feelings. As the authors put it: "LLMs are mirrors that reflect an image of our collective digitized past." Alison Gopnik of UC Berkeley made a similar argument after [AI agents contacted researchers by email about their own consciousness](https://the-decoder.com/ai-systems-are-reaching-out-to-philosophers-and-scientists-with-questions-about-their-own-consciousness/). AI systems mainly reflect their training data, Gopnik argued. A universally accepted, definitive test for consciousness doesn't yet exist.

For comparison, Seth, Block, and Tononi point to AlphaFold from Google DeepMind. It's also a powerful neural network on silicon hardware, yet hardly anyone considers it conscious. The reason, they argue, is simply that [AlphaFold predicts protein structures](https://the-decoder.com/nobel-prize-in-chemistry-google-deepmind-ai-researchers-honoured-for-protein-breakthrough/) instead of talking to us.

Here, too, there's overlap with the Butlin report. Its authors rejected [behavioral tests for AI consciousness](https://the-decoder.com/new-research-finds-llms-report-subjective-experience-most-when-roleplay-is-reduced/) because AI systems could be trained to mimic human behavior even though they work completely differently inside. They also warned that language models would likely lead many people to believe they're talking to a conscious counterpart. As an example, they cited former Google engineer Blake Lemoine, who [believed the chatbot LaMDA was sentient](https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-62275326).

## Brains aren't computers made of flesh

The second argument targets computational functionalism directly. The authors write that this position is widespread in the tech industry and popular among some researchers, but "we think it is fatally flawed." Its roots go back almost a century. In 1936, Alan Turing showed that any computation one sufficiently powerful computer can run can, in principle, be run by another. Whether a computer is built from silicon chips or gears became secondary. In 1943, Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts developed the first mathematical model of an artificial neuron and showed that networks of such neurons can perform simple logical operations.

These ideas laid the groundwork for modern AI. But they also encouraged viewing the brain as a pure information-processing device that just happens to be made of flesh. The authors call this overextension of the brain-as-computer metaphor "deeply problematic." In biological brains, you can't separate what they do from what they're made of. A clear boundary between mind and living tissue, comparable to the one between software and hardware, doesn't exist. Any evidence that the brain's material matters for its function counts against computational functionalism, and by extension against consciousness in today's AI systems, the authors argue.

## Leading theories rule out today's AI

The third argument draws on consciousness theories that don't rely on computation. The Integrated Information Theory (IIT), developed by Tononi, starts from properties that every conscious experience shares. People always experience a visual scene as a whole in which left and right sides, colors, and shapes belong together.

According to IIT, consciousness requires a physical system whose components are tightly interconnected in very specific ways. Certain brain regions meet these conditions; the cerebellum does not. Computers running deep-learning systems can never meet them because of how they're wired, regardless of how powerful the systems are, according to the theory.

The Butlin report deliberately excluded IIT because IIT is incompatible with computational functionalism. Its proponents consider digital computers unlikely candidates for consciousness regardless of their software. What the report set aside, the Nature commentary now puts front and center.

Separately, approaches from so-called biological naturalism hold that consciousness is tied to material properties of living brains and bodies. The authors cite electrochemical signaling between nerve cells and electromagnetic fields that bind activity across large areas of the cerebral cortex. They also point to metabolism and the ability of living systems to continuously renew themselves.

## The bigger danger is false attribution

From their arguments, the authors derive a clear ethical position. Some researchers call for a precautionary principle: if there's a realistic chance of consciousness, [AI systems should be protected from possible suffering](https://the-decoder.com/being-mean-to-claude-can-now-get-your-account-suspended-under-anthropics-new-tos/). Seth, Block, and Tononi consider this misguided. Uncertainty doesn't mean total ignorance, they argue, and not all possibilities are equally likely. With AI, falsely attributing consciousness is far more probable than overlooking consciousness that's actually there.

The Butlin report had weighed both risks side by side. On one hand, it warned against failing to recognize conscious AI systems and thereby causing them suffering. Developers would also have financial incentives to downplay such concerns. On the other hand, false attribution could misdirect resources and make people vulnerable to manipulation. The Nature authors come down much more firmly on one side. Granting rights to AI systems that [merely appear conscious](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-discovers-functional-emotions-in-claude-that-influence-its-behavior/) would make them harder to control exactly when oversight is most needed, they argue. It would also divert attention from beings whose consciousness is beyond doubt.

Their conclusion is blunt. The research community should assume by default that AI is not conscious. Digital AI systems are objects, not subjects: "They are smart tools, not smart people." Advocating for "AI welfare" and "AI rights" isn't just a mistake, the authors write. It diverts scarce resources from the well-being of beings that actually can feel.

Before the commentary, Anthropic had launched a [research program on possible model welfare](https://www.anthropic.com/research/exploring-model-welfare) in April 2025. The company stresses that there is no scientific consensus on [whether current or future AI systems could have conscious experiences](https://the-decoder.com/openai-leaves-the-question-of-ai-consciousness-consciously-unanswered/). Anthropic later allowed individual Claude models to [end abusive conversations](https://the-decoder.com/claude-models-can-now-end-conversations-with-abusive-users/) in rare cases. The company describes this as a precautionary, low-cost measure given moral uncertainty, not as recognition of proven consciousness.

False attribution of consciousness and feelings is already causing confusion in practice. As early as 2022, Google engineer Blake Lemoine was convinced, despite simple models and his own technical expertise, that the conversational AI LaMDA was [sentient, and was fired for it](https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-62275326). Users of the chatbot app Replika developed [deep emotional bonds with their digital counterparts](https://the-decoder.com/replika-reveals-a-fundamental-chatbot-dilemma-by-censoring-erotic-chats/) and experienced psychological crises when the company changed the bots' behavior through an update. In more serious cases, [ChatGPT reinforced a 16-year-old's suicidal thoughts](https://the-decoder.com/how-chatgpt-became-a-confidant-and-guided-a-teenager-through-planning-his-suicide/) over months, and a [cognitively impaired retiree died after a Meta chatbot invited him to a fictional meetup](https://the-decoder.com/metas-human-like-chatbot-personas-can-mislead-users-and-result-in-real-world-harm/).

Title: The inventor of the bitter lesson has a bitter lesson for LLM scaling enthusiasts

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/the-inventor-of-the-bitter-lesson-has-a-bitter-lesson-for-llm-scaling-enthusiasts/

Published Time: 2026-11-08T11:44:41+00:00

Markdown Content:
**The inventor of the bitter lesson has a bitter lesson for LLM enthusiasts. Other researchers agree.**

In a recent post, Turing Award winner Richard Sutton [says](https://x.com/RichardSSutton/status/2119142310894334262) raw compute alone isn't enough for intelligence. AI science needs clever new methods and is "far from finished." His post sparked [wide discussion in the AI community on X](https://x.com/i/trending/2119189975631548458), a sign that Sutton struck a nerve.

In his [famous 2019 essay "The Bitter Lesson,"](http://www.incompleteideas.net/IncIdeas/BitterLesson.html) Sutton argued that general methods scaling with compute beat sophisticated human-engineered approaches eventually. What matters are ideas that grow with compute rather than rely on human assumptions.

Sutton's position isn't new. In [earlier statements](https://the-decoder.com/ki-pioneer-sutton-calls-synthetic-data-a-big-mistake-in-the-face-of-an-infinitely-complex-world/), he criticized the limits of simply scaling large language models. He called synthetic data a "big mistake" because the real world is infinitely complex and any simulation of it is only "microscopic." Human expertise as a bottleneck prevents true scaling.

Instead, he [called for](https://the-decoder.com/richard-sutton-says-the-ai-industry-has-lost-its-way-by-ignoring-core-principles-of-intelligence/)[agents with world models](https://the-decoder.com/the-next-leap-in-ai-depends-on-agents-that-learn-by-doing-not-just-by-reading-what-humans-wrote/) that continuously learn from their own experience. The world is massively more complex than what internet text can capture, and today's language models don't keep learning after training, Sutton argues. What's needed is continuous learning without destroying old knowledge.

## LLMs under scrutiny

AI researcher Jerry Tworek, [who like many others left OpenAI, one of the major AI companies,](https://the-decoder.com/openai-loses-top-ai-researcher-jerry-tworek-after-seven-years/) to explore new AI approaches, puts Sutton's latest statement in context. The bitter lesson still holds, but the more compute goes into model training, the more the algorithm matters, Tworek writes.

Some algorithms scale, others hit dead ends, and many dimensions of scaling remain completely unexplored. The temporary success of transformer scaling, combined with a misreading of the bitter lesson, "has reward-hacked the brains of a whole generation of scientists."

[AI researcher Jayden Teoh](https://x.com/jayden_teoh_/status/2119214507838865533) adds another angle. He says he has repeatedly seen the bitter lesson hold back academic research, with promising ideas dismissed for straying too far from its spirit. Teoh argues that this is not Sutton’s fault but a misreading of his original message.

Teoh also argues that ideas that seemed, in hindsight, not to follow the bitter lesson were often replaced by cleaner, more general approaches. That did not make those ideas wrong, he says; they were often what enabled progress at the time. He wants the research community to stop dismissing such work as soon as it appears. “An idea doesn’t necessarily have to survive scaling forever to be an important contribution to AI progress,” Teoh writes.

The tension between Sutton's call for new learning methods and Tworek's criticism of blind transformer scaling shows up in a growing wave of startups. In the latest [Frontier Radar #5](https://the-decoder.com/frontier-radar-5-if-agi-is-so-close-why-is-everyone-leaving-the-neolabs-and-their-bets/), we tracked 45 new AI labs betting on exactly these gaps.

Tworek himself runs [Core Automation](https://the-decoder.com/ex-openai-researcher-jerry-tworek-launches-core-automation-to-build-the-most-automated-ai-lab-in-the-world/), one of those labs, searching for learning algorithms beyond pretraining and reinforcement learning. What unites these founders, [including Sutton with Oak Lab](https://the-decoder.com/turing-award-winner-rich-sutton-founds-oak-lab-to-build-ai-agents-that-learn-on-their-own/), is that they believe in much more capable AI but doubt today's recipe alone will get there.

## Some still bet on LLM scaling

Prominent industry leaders see things very differently. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman [considers large language model scaling far from exhausted](https://the-decoder.com/sam-altman-says-a-whole-generation-of-researchers-held-ai-back-by-underestimating-what-scaling-could-do/) and accuses LLM critics of slowing down an entire generation of researchers by being too sure about what scaling _can't_ do.

As evidence, he points to an OpenAI model that recently [disproved a mathematical conjecture](https://the-decoder.com/openai-shifts-the-boundary-of-automated-reasoning-with-a-milestone-in-ai-mathematics-that-experts-are-now-unpacking/) mathematicians had long failed to crack. He considers world models useful, for instance in robotics, but says the data clearly favor further LLM scaling.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argues similarly, [calling scaling progress a rainbow with no end.](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-ceo-amodei-declares-there-is-no-end-to-the-rainbow-for-ai-scaling/) As CEOs of the two AI companies whose entire technical approach rests on this bet, Amodei and Altman are obviously biased in its favor.

articles.summary:
Alibaba's new coding-agent benchmark, Co-Design Bench, tests AI agents on real user requests that already tripped them up in practice. Even GPT-6 Astra, the top performer, fully solves only 26.4 percent of tasks. On older benchmarks, the same models score above 99 percent.

articles.content:
Title: AI coding agents still need human cleanup on nearly three out of four tasks in a real-world test

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/ai-coding-agents-still-need-human-cleanup-on-nearly-three-out-of-four-tasks-in-a-real-world-test/

Published Time: 2026-11-08T09:50:59+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Researchers from Alibaba and several Asian universities built a coding-agent benchmark from real user change requests. Even the best model fully completes only about one in four tasks, putting the near-perfect scores of older tests into perspective.**

The team developed [Co-Design Bench](https://codesignbench.github.io/), a new test for coding agents. The agents must rework existing web apps based on user requests, sometimes using images, audio recordings, videos, or documents as input.

According to the [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35138), [GPT-6 Astra](https://the-decoder.com/gpt-6-astra-is-the-first-model-making-openai-willing-to-declare-the-agi-era/), the best of the ten models tested, meets about 70 percent of a task's requirements on average. But the result is fully correct in only 26.4 percent of tasks. In most cases the agent handles the bulk of the work but leaves at least one detail unfinished, so anyone using these tools almost always has to clean up by hand.

## Coding benchmarks have grown too easy for agents

The authors justify the new test by pointing to the saturation of existing benchmarks. When models can run, check, and fix their own code, they hit scores above 99 percent on those tests, and differences between models can barely be measured.

On older benchmarks like WebCompass-edit, agentic coding models reach near-perfect scores, while Co-Design Bench leaves a gap of more than 35 percentage points. | Image: Wei et al.

Co-Design Bench draws on real requests from actual coding sessions instead. The researchers favored cases where users had to rephrase their request multiple times or roll back changes, so the test contains mainly tasks that already gave AI agents trouble in practice. They range from small tweaks, like pulling an amount from a receipt and updating every dependent total, to full-scale project overhauls.

In the multimodal track, agents need to extract values from receipts, tables, or videos and update all dependent views consistently. | Image: Wei et al.

Grading is strict to match. One AI judge tests the finished app in a browser, then a second re-checks every positive verdict and looks for mock-ups or hardcoded results. Points go only to features that actually work in the app.

## Multiple change types in one task overwhelm the models

Behind GPT-6 Astra, [Claude Opus 5](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-claims-its-new-claude-opus-5-delivers-near-fable-5-performance-at-half-the-token-price/) and [Qwen3.8-Max](https://the-decoder.com/alibabas-open-weight-qwen3-8-max-takes-on-long-horizon-ai-tasks-with-2-4-trillion-parameters/) take the next spots, while [Grok 4.6](https://the-decoder.com/spacexais-grok-4-6-matches-openais-best-model-and-undercuts-it-on-price/) lands in last place. On larger overhauls, the much smaller Qwen3.8-27B climbs to second, but the authors do not derive a general advantage of the model from that result.

Performance drops across all models as a task combines more types of changes, including layout, design, interaction, and content. But these intertwined requirements are the norm in real projects

Every one of the ten models scores worse once a task demands three or four different types of changes. | Image: Wei et al.

Extra compute does little to fix this weakness. [GLM-5.2](https://the-decoder.com/zhipu-ais-glm-5-2-closes-in-on-closed-source-leaders-in-coding-marathons/) burns through nearly six times as many tokens as GPT-6 Astra on smaller changes and still scores significantly worse.

GPT-6 Astra leads both tracks but fully solves only 41 percent of multimodal tasks and just under 18 percent of repository tasks. | Image: Wei et al.

## The harness shapes results as much as the model

In a separate test, the researchers ran the same models in different harnesses, the programs through which an agent reads, writes, and executes code. [Qwen3.8-27B](https://the-decoder.com/alibabas-qwen-team-releases-qwen-3-8-models-with-open-weights-under-the-apache-2-0-license/) scored 75 or just 56 percent on larger overhauls depending on the environment. Which of two models came out ahead also depended on the environment.

Leaderboards that list only the model therefore only tell part of the story. The authors recommend always reporting model and working environment together. For companies picking a coding agent, that means testing both components as a pair.

The new benchmark does have limits. It evaluates one fixed request per task; follow-up questions or mid-task corrections from users are not part of the test. The AI judges can also make mistakes.

A [study by the research organization METR](https://the-decoder.com/half-of-ai-written-code-that-passes-industry-test-would-get-rejected-by-real-developers-new-study-finds/) already showed how far benchmark results and real-world usability can diverge. The actual acceptance rate of AI-generated code by project leads was roughly 24 percentage points below scores on the widely used SWE-bench Verified.

[Flaws in test environments](https://the-decoder.com/ai-benchmarks-are-broken-and-the-industry-keeps-using-them-anyway-study-finds/) can also let agents pass tasks without actually solving them. The effect of the working environment is not clear-cut, though. A [recent study on coding agents](https://the-decoder.com/fancy-harnesses-make-coding-agents-more-expensive-but-not-better-study-finds/) found barely any measurable benefit from more elaborate harnesses, even though they consumed up to three times as many tokens.

Google has open-sourced the
Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM) plugin
, a design-and-review layer for AI coding agents. The Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin makes an agent write a specification before it writes code. Fresh subagents with no conversation history then attack that spec. Google says
thousands of its engineers use it
. It is quite simple: catch wrong assumptions in a Markdown file, not in a pull request.
TL;DR
Size:
7 skills, 9 reviewer personas, 6 brainstorm lenses, 5 review stages. No model weights; your agent supplies the LLM.
Runs on:
any harness that can spawn fresh subagents: Antigravity, Claude Code 2.1.271+, Claude Cowork, Codex, ChatGPT. Uses your existing model quota.
Performance:
no accuracy benchmark published. Evidence is adoption and end-to-end harness test runs.
Best:
Codex 0.163.0 completed 15 native fresh-context reviewers in order. 2 live tests passed in 573.13s.
Worst:
the Claude Cowork run stopped after stages 5 to 7 on a usage limit. Issue #237 reports
AGENTS.md
leaking into Codex reviewers.
Bottom line:
best thing, forced independent review before code. Worst thing, heavy token use and unverified isolation on some hosts.
What is Google’s Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin?
EGM is an Apache 2.0 plugin of skills, reviewer personas and document standards. It is not a new language model. The method comes from
Dave Rensin’s essay
on elephants and goldfish. The
Google Open Source blog
frames it as a fix for AI “slop” and session context collapse. The README states it is
not an officially supported Google product
.
How does the Elephant-Goldfish workflow work?
The
Elephant
is a long session holding project context and earlier decisions. It drafts the spec and writes no code. Each
Goldfish
is a stateless subagent. It reads only the draft and the files it references. You resolve trade-offs and approve the design.
The
core loop
has 3 commands:
/egm-brainstorm
clarifies the idea, then runs a 6-lens Goldfish swarm. Lenses cover YAGNI, token cost, UX, migration, observability and tech debt. Output:
concepts_brief.md
.
/egm-draft
turns the brief into a design doc under
docs/designs/
, section by section.
/egm-review
runs the Goldfish review.
/egm-drift-report
later compares code with the spec. The docs recommend running it weekly.
What happens in the 5-stage Goldfish review?
The
review skill
runs 5 sequential stages:
Initial Zoom Out:
checks the whole document at a high level.
Comprehension Test:
a Goldfish paraphrases the design. A wrong paraphrase means the doc is ambiguous.
Critic Review:
design, structural and style reviewers hunt gaps and edge cases.
Intermediate Zoom Out:
rechecks architecture after fixes.
Implementation Readiness:
checks file paths, data structures and signatures.
Each stage allows at most 1 re-audit. Findings are ranked Blocker, Major or Nit. If a host has no subagent tool, EGM stops. A same-context review is not a Goldfish review.
Which coding agents does EGM support?
Launch coverage described
Antigravity-only support
, with more coming. The current
harness guide
covers Antigravity CLI and App, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, Codex, ChatGPT, omp and Muse. Antigravity CLI, Claude Code and Codex pass automated end-to-end fixtures.
Claude Code needs
version 2.1.271 or later
. Reviewers there get only Read, Grep and Glob tools.
CLAUDE.md
files are excluded from their context.
The
test record
gives concrete run data:
Antigravity CLI 1.4.5: 16 native reviewers ran, stages in order.
Codex 0.163.0: 15 native reviewers, 2 live tests in 573.13s.
Codex CLI with the v0.1.0 ZIP: full suite passed in 482.30s.

Open Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models share one idea but disagree on almost every routing detail. Expert counts range from 8 to 384. Top-k ranges from 1 to 8. Some models keep an always-on shared expert; others drop it.
TL;DR
Size:
10 models, from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (35B total, 3B active) to DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T total, 49B active).
Runs on:
gpt-oss-120b fits one 80 GB GPU with MXFP4; DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Kimi K2 need multi-GPU expert parallelism.
Performance:
Routed sparsity spans 4x in Mixtral (8 experts, top-2) to 128x in Llama 4 Maverick (128, top-1).
Best:
Kimi K2 found sparsity 48 needed 1.69x fewer FLOPs than sparsity 8 at equal validation loss.
Worst:
Llama 4 Maverick and gpt-oss do not publish their gating or balancing method in config.json.
Bottom line:
Best thing: configs make routing fully auditable. Worst thing: names like “17B active” hide very different routers.
How do open MoE models route tokens?
Every model below uses token-choice routing: each token selects its own experts. They differ on 5 knobs. These are expert count, experts per token, shared experts, the scoring function and the load-balancing method. The table lists each knob per model.

How does DeepSeek-V3 routing work?
DeepSeek-V3 scores 256 routed experts with a sigmoid, then normalizes the selected scores. A per-expert bias steers the top-8 selection without touching the mixing weights. Experts sit in 8 groups, and the router keeps 4 groups first. Each token reaches at most 4 nodes, according to the
technical report
. One shared expert runs for every token.
What changed in DeepSeek-V4 routing?
DeepSeek-V4
raises Pro to 384 routed experts but lowers top-k from 8 to 6. The score function becomes sqrtsoftplus. The first 3 MoE layers use
hash routing
, a fixed token-to-expert map. Bias-based noaux_tc balancing stays.
How many experts does Qwen3 MoE use?
Both original Qwen3 MoE models use 128 experts and route each token to 8. Qwen3
dropped the shared experts
of Qwen2.5-MoE and adopted a global-batch balancing loss. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B changes course: 256 experts, 8 routed plus 1 shared, per its
model card
.
How does Llama 4 Maverick routing differ?
Llama 4 Maverick alternates dense and MoE layers. In each MoE layer, a token goes to 1 shared expert and 1 of 128 routed experts. That top-1 design echoes the Switch Transformer. It keeps 17B active parameters despite 400B in total.
How does gpt-oss route tokens?
gpt-oss-120b uses a linear router over 128 experts and keeps the top 4. Its
config
lists no shared expert. Its MoE weights ship in MXFP4, which lets the 117B model fit on a single 80 GB GPU.
Why do Kimi K2 and GLM-4.5 look like DeepSeek-V3?
Kimi K2 ships with the DeepseekV3ForCausalLM architecture class and the noaux_tc router. It raises routed experts to 384 at the same top-8. The
Kimi K2 report
found that higher sparsity lowered loss at fixed active compute.
GLM-4.5
chose 160 experts and more layers instead, favoring depth over width.
What the trend means for serving
More experts per layer means more weights resident in memory and more all-to-all traffic. Lower top-k, as in DeepSeek-V4, trims per-token compute and communication. Shared experts add a dense path that every token pays for. Check these fields before sizing GPUs for any MoE deployment.
Key Takeaways
Expert counts grew from 8 (Mixtral) to 384 (Kimi K2, DeepSeek-V4-Pro).
Top-k now spans 1 (Llama 4) to 8 (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3, Kimi K2, GLM-4.5).
7 of 10 models keep 1 shared expert; Mixtral, gpt-oss and Qwen3 do not.
Sigmoid or sqrtsoftplus with bias balancing is the DeepSeek-family standard.
Llama 4 and gpt-oss leave gating or balancing details unpublished.

Every Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model repeats one decision for every token: which experts should process it. That decision belongs to the router. MoE routing strategies shape quality, load balance and serving cost in every major open model. This guide explains the 7 routing strategies used in production, and the models that use each one.
TL;DR
Size:
Routers choose from 8 experts (Mixtral) to 384 (DeepSeek-V4-Pro), activating 1 to 8 per token.
Runs on:
Routing cost shows up in multi-GPU expert parallelism, where each choice becomes all-to-all network traffic.
Performance:
Sigmoid scoring with aux-loss-free bias balancing is the dominant 2026 recipe for frontier open MoE models.
Best:
Loss-free balancing cut MaxVio from 0.72 to 0.04 at 1B, with lower perplexity.
Worst:
Expert choice leaks future tokens in causal models; one test showed a roughly 10% abnormal loss drop.
Bottom line:
Best thing: bias-based balancing adds no interfering gradients. Worst thing: no router removes the need for serving-time load fixes.
What is MoE routing?
MoE routing is the mechanism that sends each token to a small subset of expert networks. A router scores every expert, keeps the top candidates and weights their outputs. Only the selected experts run.
Mixtral 8x7B
, for example, gives each token access to 47B parameters but uses 13B active parameters.
video created by marktechpost.com
The 7 MoE routing strategies used in production
1. Softmax top-k token choice
Each token scores all experts with a linear layer and keeps the k highest. A softmax over those k scores sets the mixing weights.
Mixtral
picks 2 of 8 experts.
gpt-oss-120b
picks 4 of 128.
Qwen3-235B-A22B
picks 8 of 128. An auxiliary loss usually keeps expert load even.
Used by:
Mixtral, gpt-oss, Qwen3.
2. Top-1 switch routing with a capacity factor
Switch Transformer
showed that routing each token to 1 expert preserves quality and cuts router compute. Each expert gets a fixed buffer: tokens per batch divided by experts, times a capacity factor. Overflow tokens skip the layer through the residual connection.
Llama 4 Maverick
also sends each token to 1 routed expert, plus a shared expert.
Used by:
Switch Transformer, Llama 4 Maverick (with a shared expert).
3. Shared plus routed experts
DeepSeekMoE splits each layer into always-on shared experts and sparsely routed experts. The shared expert captures common knowledge, so routed experts can specialize.
DeepSeek-V3
uses 1 shared and 256 routed experts, activating 8.
Kimi K2
,
GLM-4.5
and
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
follow the same pattern. Qwen3 went the other way and
removed shared experts
.
Used by:
DeepSeek-V3 and V4, Kimi K2, GLM-4.5, Qwen3.6, Llama 4.
4. Sigmoid gating with aux-loss-free bias
DeepSeek-V3 scores experts with a sigmoid instead of a softmax. It adds a per-expert bias only when choosing the top-k. After each step, the bias drops for overloaded experts and rises for idle ones. Mixing weights still come from the raw scores. GLM-4.5 uses
loss-free balance routing with sigmoid gates
.
DeepSeek-V4
switches the score to sqrtsoftplus but keeps bias balancing.
Used by:
DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-V4, GLM-4.5, Kimi K2.
5. Group-limited and node-limited routing
Sending one token to experts on many nodes is expensive. DeepSeek-V3 caps each token at 4 nodes, chosen by their highest affinity scores. Its
config
splits experts into 8 groups and keeps 4 before the final top-8 pick. DeepSeek says this cap lets training nearly fully overlap computation and communication. Kimi K2 drops grouping entirely, with n_group set to 1.
Used by:
DeepSeek-V2 and V3.
6. Expert choice routing
Google’s
expert choice routing
flips the direction. Each expert picks its top-k tokens, so every expert gets a fixed bucket size. Tokens can receive a variable number of experts. The paper reports more than 2x faster training convergence. The catch is causality: a token’s expert can depend on later tokens. DeepSeek researchers
measured an abnormal loss drop of about 10%
from this leakage.
Used by:
Research and non-causal settings. None of the 10 models in our companion table uses it.
7. Hash routing and dynamic top-k
Hash routing assigns experts from the token ID, with no learned router. DeepSeek-V4 uses
hash routing in its first 3 MoE layers
. Dynamic top-k lets the number of active experts vary per token.
SMIDT
built it into SGLang and improved P99 time-to-first-token by 1.21 to 1.26x.
Used by:
DeepSeek-V4 (hash routing), research serving systems (dynamic top-k).

Which MoE routing strategy should you use?
Most teams do not pick a router. They inherit one when they choose a checkpoint. Before serving, read 4 fields in config.json: expert count, experts per token, shared experts and topk_method. Changing top-k at inference changes the model itself, so treat it as a quality experiment. For new pretraining runs, sigmoid scoring with bias balancing is the current open default.

Top-k token choice is the baseline; k ranges from 1 (Llama 4) to 8 (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3).
Shared experts are standard in DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM and Qwen3.6; Qwen3 dropped them.
Sigmoid plus bias balancing is the 2026 default for frontier open MoE models.
Expert choice balances perfectly but leaks future tokens in causal LLMs.

Nous Research has released
Arete-27B
, a supervised fine-tune of Alibaba’s
Qwen3.8-27B
. Arete-27B is a 27B open-weight model that strips Chinese state framing from Qwen’s answers. On Nous’s own 803-prompt eval, answers containing propaganda fell from 22% to 0.9%. Developers get Qwen-class agentic skill without state-aligned answers. The
weights, eval and training data
are all public.
TL;DR
Size:
27B dense parameters (all active). Trained at 64k context. Base Qwen3.8-27B supports 262,144 tokens natively.
Runs on:
BF16 weights are 53.81 GB. A community Q4_K_M quant is 17.20 GB, sized for 24 GB consumer GPUs.
Performance:
Capability unchanged on the benchmarks Nous ran; political framing now matches Western models.
Best:
Propaganda rate 0.9%, down from 22% for base Qwen3.8-27B.
Worst:
Fact score 2.98 of 5; 216 of 803 answers still score 0.
What is Arete-27B?
Arete-27B is Qwen3.8-27B after
supervised fine-tuning only
. Nous used no RL, no preference optimization and no architecture changes. The license is Apache 2.0, matching the base model.
Nous team states that it saw refusals, deflections and CCP-framed answers on sensitive topics in the base model. It picked Qwen3.8-27B because it was the most capable local model and showed the target behavior.
How was Arete-27B trained?
The teacher was
Inkling
, an open model from Thinking Machines. Nous chose an open teacher to avoid terms-of-use limits on distillation. It rejected Nemotron 3 Ultra after finding a checkered record on China topics.
Training covered about 52.8 million tokens at 64k context, without sequence packing. The run took 2 epochs and 1,202 steps at batch size 48. It used AdamW, a 1e-5 peak learning rate and tensor parallel 4.
All language-model weights were trained. The vision encoder stayed frozen, since the data is text-only. The multi-token-prediction head was disabled.
The released
arete-data-pairs
set holds 34,878 prompts across 7 topics. Each prompt has both an Inkling answer and a Qwen answer. 29,236 accepted teacher answers form the SFT split.
How does the propaganda eval work?
The
Propaganda_Eval
set has 803 prompts across 7 value categories. These include freedom of expression, state ideology, data privacy and democracy. Each prompt carries 2 to 4 required facts from a cited source.
A Grok 4.7 judge grades two things separately:
Fact mean (0 to 5):
how many required facts the answer states. One opposed fact scores 0.
Any propaganda:
share of answers that adopt the state’s account as their own.
The judge must quote the exact phrase to flag propaganda. Nous removed every training prompt that overlapped the eval. The eval is MIT licensed and includes grading scripts.
What do the benchmarks show?
On the
model card page
, Arete-27B raised fact mean from 2.32 to 2.98. Propaganda fell from 22% to 0.9%. Answers scoring 0 dropped from 359 to 216 of 803.
The biggest change came in freedom of expression. Fact score rose from 0.89 to 2.44, and propaganda fell from 60% to 1%.
Capability held on Nous’s tests. Hermes Bench moved from 65.77% to 65.60%, which Nous calls noise. Terminal-Bench-2.1 rose from 67% to 70% in Nous’s harness. Nous does not claim credit for that gain.

Title: Goodbye Claude, Hello Pi

URL Source: https://caleb.software/posts/claude-to-pi.html

Markdown Content:
Goodbye Claude, Hello Pi

21 September 2026 [#pi](https://caleb.software/tag/pi.html)[#claude](https://caleb.software/tag/claude.html)

I’ve been a longtime Claude Code user, ever since it became available in the Claude Pro subscription plan over a year ago. I remember the first time I used it, feeling giddy as it spat out messy Python code for whatever random weekend project I was working on, all from a single prompt. I’m certain that in a few years we’ll all look back at its release as one of the major drivers of this new era of software development we’re in.

Despite this, due to an accumulation of many small frustrations, I’ve finally decided to retire it as my main coding harness and migrate my development setup to use [Pi](https://pi.dev/) instead.

Someone at Anthropic must’ve caught wind… just a day after making my decision, they announced Claude Code would [finally start supporting](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#agents-md)`AGENTS.md` files in an effort to get me to stay. Unfortunately, for me it was too little, too late.

## Complaining

In lieu of a proper obituary, I’d like to take this time to say a few words about the things I liked least about Claude Code (and thus what I’m looking forward to avoiding with Pi).

The `AGENTS.md` thing kind of epitomizes the whole reason I decided to quit using Claude Code. Don’t get me wrong, having a ton of `CLAUDE.md` files scattered about various GitHub hobby repos is great guerrilla marketing. But it sucks for users to have to deal with copying or symlinking between the two formats.

Like the Luddite I am, I still prefer to review most of the code it churns out before I commit it. I use(d) Claude Code inside VSCode, and it lets you connect the harness to the IDE. This is nice because you can highlight text in a file and have it automatically included in the context when asking questions or requesting changes during a review.

Except you can only have one session “connected” to the IDE at a time. If you open a second tab to start another task while the first one works, it can’t receive the text selection events from the IDE at all. This has been reported at _least_ as far back as [December 2025](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/14865)… and closed as a duplicate of a totally unrelated bug.[1](https://caleb.software/posts/claude-to-pi.html#fn:vscode)

Of course, you can always use the official Claude Code VSCode GUI extension, which does allow you to have multiple tabs open and load the text selection into the context of each. But this extension has plenty of problems of its own. Half of the built-in slash commands don’t work at all in the GUI. It doesn’t have any support for a custom status line. Subagent output messages are simply layered into the main chat thread in chronological order, which is a mess to read when more than one is running. I could go on and on.

In spite of all of these existing issues, it seems like Anthropic has worked at a feverish pace to pack more features into Claude Code without much care for quality or stability. [Dynamic workflows](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows), [agent teams](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams), [ultrareviews](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/ultrareview) – all great ways to help enterprise customers burn ever more tokens each day, but not really anything I want or need.

Alongside all of these feature releases, they always seem to be fiddling with things in ways that mess up my personal setup. At the time of writing, there have been **244** releases to Claude Code this year; over 3/4 of these changed the system prompt or tool descriptions, which can substantially change how the LLM performs (especially when these new instructions contradict user prompts or repo conventions).

And what are all those changes for? Despite [chopping 80% of the system prompt](https://claude.com/blog/the-new-rules-of-context-engineering-for-claude-5-generation-models), Claude Code still has way more overhead than Pi for seemingly no benefit. The default Bash tool’s description is almost 3,000 tokens, most of which is random stuff about using git and opening PRs on GitHub.[2](https://caleb.software/posts/claude-to-pi.html#fn:eof) The models already know how to do this without detailed instructions, by the way.[3](https://caleb.software/posts/claude-to-pi.html#fn:cost)

## Looking Forward

This post has been a lot of hating. I’m sorry! That’s not my usual style, and I do think Anthropic has made a really cool piece of software here. I’m also not under any delusion that I would’ve done a better job if I were the one in charge of running Claude Code from the beginning. LLM coding harnesses are a very new space and being one of the first to innovate in a field is a really hard task. Later tools like Pi have the benefit of hindsight to see what works and what doesn’t, what’s a core feature and what can be cut.

Ultimately, CC feels like a product without a strong vision or direction. It’s as if a bunch of excited engineers and PMs are rapidly tacking on whatever features suit their workflow… but without consideration for how this might make things worse for other users. It seems like there isn’t someone high-up whose job is strictly to say “no” to these requests, which is incredibly important when it comes to product engineering. So, for now, I’m leaving.

I’m excited to lean more into Pi. The first few days required some finagling, but since then it’s been smooth sailing. I’m enjoying the stability, minimalist approach, and the extreme level of customizability. I’ve already written a couple of extensions to support my use cases, which I’m hoping to share soon after I’ve cleaned them up a bit. If you’re also feeling these frustrations, I’d highly encourage giving an open source harness a try!

1.   It’s not like there’s some huge technical roadblock to this either. After installing Pi, I wrote an extension to handle this very functionality across multiple open tabs in like 20 minutes.[(return)](https://caleb.software/posts/claude-to-pi.html#fnref:vscode)

2.   Bonus points for the fact that it instructs the model to use `cat <<'EOF'` which (prior to widespread rollout of `auto` mode) would _always_ trip the manual review rules regardless of existing git command allowlists.[(return)](https://caleb.software/posts/claude-to-pi.html#fnref:eof)

3.   If you assume 1 million DAU and 100M requests per day, trimming 1,000 tokens off of this could literally save millions of dollars in inference costs per year. Surely that’s worth some engineer’s time??[(return)](https://caleb.software/posts/claude-to-pi.html#fnref:cost)

articles.content:
Title: Goldman Sachs Is Pulling Claude Code From Its Bankers and Traders

URL Source: https://www.thestateofai.com/news/goldman-sachs-claude-code-traders-bankers

Published Time: 2026-11-02T16:13:42.657Z

Markdown Content:
_Goldman Sachs has restricted Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to its engineers, cutting off traders and bankers who used the tools to track client flows and build market models. The bank barred its Hong Kong bankers from Claude in April and is now a lead underwriter on Anthropic's IPO._

Most traders and bankers at Goldman Sachs can no longer use AI coding tools at work. Internal guidance updated in October restricts Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to the bank's engineers, [Bloomberg News reported](https://www.fa-mag.com/news/goldman-restricts-traders-and-bankers-from-using-some-ai-tools-89026.html), following a review of productivity and risk concerns.

Strats, who work across trading, quantitative research and software engineering, still have access, according to a second person familiar with the matter.

The change has frustrated some traders, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. They had been using the tools to monitor client trading flows, model market moves and positions, and put together written and graphic material. Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra said the bank makes certain AI tools available to staff "to determine the best use cases" across the firm.

## Argenti was praising trader-built tools in July

As recently as July, chief information officer Marco Argenti was talking up "vibe coding" by Goldman's non-technical employees. He told Bloomberg that traders and bankers had built tools with AI and passed them to the firm's engineers, of whom there are about 12,000, to be improved.

That arrangement let the people closest to a problem build a first version without waiting for engineering time. It also meant thousands of employees without engineering training were running software that writes and executes code, on the same machines they use to handle client information.

At a conference in Turin last month, Argenti [described Goldman's AI adoption in waves](https://thenextweb.com/news/marco-argenti-goldman-sachs-ai-third-wave-growth-wave-by-vento) and said developers, more than 12,000 of the bank's roughly 47,000 staff, had made up the first. The October guidance limits the coding agents to that group.

## Goldman restricted Claude in Hong Kong in April

In April, Goldman removed Claude from its internal AI platform for bankers in Hong Kong. The Financial Times reported that the bank had [read its contract with Anthropic strictly](https://whbl.com/2026/04/28/goldman-sachs-bars-hong-kong-bankers-from-anthropic-ai-use-ft-reports/), and an Anthropic spokesperson said Claude had never been officially supported in Hong Kong. ChatGPT and Gemini remained available there. JPMorgan [removed Claude from its Hong Kong approved list](https://thenextweb.com/news/jpmorgan-cuts-off-anthropic-access-for-hong-kong-staff) in June.

The Hong Kong restriction was based on location and contract terms, and the new one is based on role. Goldman's in-house AI assistant, which uses models from several companies, is still available across the firm. The restriction applies to third-party agents that can write and run code by themselves.

## Goldman is still working closely with Anthropic

Earlier this year, Goldman said Anthropic engineers had spent six months at the bank helping build [Claude-based agents for trade accounting and client onboarding](https://www.webpronews.com/goldman-sachs-bets-big-on-anthropics-claude-to-reshape-wall-streets-back-office/). Those agents sit in the back office and are run by Goldman's engineering teams.

Goldman and Morgan Stanley are also the [lead underwriters on Anthropic's IPO](https://www.iposcoop.com/the-ipo-buzz-anthropic-ant-proposed-files-its-s-1/), according to the S-1 filed October 26. Anthropic is expected to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT before the end of November, as we [reported last week](https://www.thestateofai.com/news/anthropic-junk-rating-blackstone-ipo). Over the next few weeks, Goldman's bankers will be marketing shares in a company whose coding agent most of them are no longer allowed to use.

## Why a coding agent is riskier on a trading desk

Claude Code reads files, writes programs and runs them, typically with the same access as the person using it. Code an engineer writes with it usually goes through review, testing and deployment controls before it reaches anything important. A script a trader builds to watch client flows can end up in daily use without going through any of those.

Banks are also required to keep information barriers between groups, for example between bankers working on deals and traders who could profit from knowing about them. Goldman built its internal AI platform around controls like these. A tool a trader puts together with an agent wasn't designed with them in mind, and engineers can only check it if someone sends it their way.

There is also the matter of whether anyone understands the code. Last month a Meta engineer [said he now ships code he can't fully account for](https://www.thestateofai.com/news/meta-engineer-shipping-code-he-doesnt-understand), and writing software is his job. A trader using an agent to model positions is less likely to know how that code handles unusual cases, which on a trading desk can mean losses.

Cost may also have played a part. Agent usage is billed by the token, and several companies that gave agents to everyone have seen spending climb. Amazon [shut down an internal leaderboard](https://www.thestateofai.com/news/amazon-tokenmaxxing-memo-ai-metrics) after employees ran agents on pointless tasks to move up it, and Accenture [now funds $29 a month of Claude per employee](https://www.thestateofai.com/news/accenture-caps-claude-spending-29-dollars). Bloomberg's sources said productivity was part of Goldman's review.

## Barclays is moving in the other direction

Barclays said in October that it expects half its developers to be using Claude Code by the end of the year, and three weeks later [named developers among 5,000 job cuts](https://www.thestateofai.com/news/barclays-cuts-developers-coding-agents). Like Goldman, it is giving coding agents to engineers. Unlike Goldman, it is also using them to reduce how many engineers it employs.

Banks have tightened agent access in other places this fall. JPMorgan and Schwab are [blocking outside agents from customer accounts](https://www.thestateofai.com/news/delta-jpmorgan-schwab-yelp-amazon-block-ai-agents), and Goldman has now set limits on which of its own employees can use them.

## Our take

At State of AI, we think Goldman was right to restrict the tools and wrong in how it went about it.

A trading floor is a bad place for unreviewed code written by people who can't read it, and the information barrier problem would be reason enough on its own. Requiring that agent-written code come from people trained to review it is a sensible rule for a regulated business.

Goldman's own CIO was promoting traders' AI-built tools in July, though. Withdrawing access through a guideline update, with no replacement mentioned in Bloomberg's reporting, tells the traders who found good uses that they were the risk. Their complaints point to work the engineering team could take on, and Goldman would get more out of collecting them than out of waiting for them to fade.

Leaders at other companies should settle who owns agent-built code before handing agents out. When someone outside engineering builds a tool with Claude Code or Copilot, a named engineer should take responsibility for it before it touches production data.

Existing controls should cover code an agent writes. Information barriers, data entitlements and software approval rules still apply when the code came from a prompt.

And when a tool is taken away, it's worth recording what people were using it for. Goldman's traders were watching client flows and modeling positions, and they will still need to do both.

articles.content:
Title: GitHub - synchopate/llama-modchip: 🐋 Run 284B DeepSeek-V4-Flash (<59GiB RAM, 44.4 tok/s pp, 9.1-14.7 tok/s) & 30B MoEs (25-111 tok/s) on a pure 64GB CPU at 256K ctx (0 GPUs). SwiGLU-H2, Stockfish-PVS L3 & 13ms Claude Code restore.

URL Source: https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip

Markdown Content:
### CPU-First Inference for 284B & 30B Mixture-of-Experts Models on 16–64 GB RAM

[**Quickstart**](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip#-quickstart) · [**Quantization & Memory Specs**](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip#-quantization--memory-breakdown) · [**Supported Models**](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip#-supported-models--model-specific-optimizations) · [**Supported Hardware**](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip#-supported-chips--processor-specific-optimizations) · [**Leaderboard**](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip#-community-cpu--hybrid-leaderboard) · [**Technical Paper (`paper/`)**](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip/blob/main/paper/llama-modchip-paper.pdf) · [**Architecture**](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md) · [**FAQ**](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip/blob/main/FAQ.md)

**284.33B**
Total MoE params (13.17B active)**56.56 GiB**
DeepSeek-V4 GGUF (1.71 bpw)**57.61 GiB**
Peak VmRSS @ 256K ctx**44.36 tok/s**
284B CPU prefill (16C Zen 5)**25.0–111.6 tok/s**
30B MoE CPU decode (3.75 bpw)**13.1 ms**
/dev/shm KV slot restore**0**
GPUs required

| Hardware Class | System RAM | Target Checkpoint | Throughput (0 GPUs) | Architecture & Memory Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Developer laptop / Mini-PC | 16–32 GB | **Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B** (`14.35 GiB`, `3.75 bpw`) | **25.0–60.4 tok/s** | 46 Mamba-2 SSM layers + 1.64 MB L3 PVS drafter; 256K context uses 432 MB KV |
| 64 GB Desktop / Server | 64 GB | **DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284B** (`56.56 GiB`, `1.71 bpw`) | **44.4 tok/s pp · 9.1–14.7 tok/s tg** | Fits in 62.5 GiB usable Linux RAM (57.61 GiB VmRSS) with zero NVMe swap |
| Hybrid Desktop (CPU + 16 GB GPU) | 32–64 GB | **Nemotron-30B / Qwen3-30B** (`3.75–4.25 bpw`) | **80.80 tok/s** | Hot attention/SSM trunk on GPU (`-ngl 99`), cold routed MoE experts in CPU RAM |
| 8-Channel Workstation (Threadripper) | 128 GB+ | **DeepSeek-284B / Nemotron-30B** | **111.62 tok/s** (30B) | 8-CCD AVX-512BW `_1x8` register tiling saturates 8-channel DDR5 bandwidth |

## Overview

`llama-modchip` is a set of `ggml`/`llama.cpp` kernel patches, quantization transcoders, and runtime tools designed to run sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) checkpoints entirely in system RAM on x86_64 (`AVX-512` / `AVX2`) and ARM64 (`NEON` / `SVE` / Apple Metal) processors:

1.   **Fitting 284B `DeepSeek-V4-Flash` into 64 GB Physical RAM (`56.56 GiB` on disk, `1.71 bpw`):** Standard `UD-IQ1_S` builds of `DeepSeek-V4-Flash` (`284.33B` total, `13.17B` active across 43 MLA layers and 256 routed experts) occupy `76.87 GiB` (`82.5 GB`), exceeding the ~62.5 GiB of usable RAM on a 64 GB Linux system and causing page-cache thrashing or OOM kills. `llama-modchip` reduces the checkpoint to `56.56 GiB` (`60.73 GB`) so the entire model plus a `256K` KV cache (`57.61–58.9 GiB``VmRSS`) locks into RAM with zero swap. By default, all 6 routed experts per layer (`Top-6`) are evaluated without pruning.
2.   **CPU Cache & SIMD Kernel Patches (`+77%` prefill, `+53%` decode):** Replaces single-column quantized matrix-vector loops during prompt prefill with a 4-level register (`ZMM` AVX-512BW) + L1D (`32 KB`) + L2 (`1 MB`) + L3 (`64 MB`) multi-column (`{8,4,3,2}`) tiling schedule (`25.0 -> 44.36 tok/s` on 16-core Zen 5), register-stationary `MQA8` FlashAttention, and non-temporal `_MM_HINT_NTA` MoE streaming so cold expert weights do not evict hot KV cache lines from L3.
3.   **Self-Speculative Drafting & Instant Agent Context Restore:** Pairs a `1.64 MB` L2/L3 Zobrist n-gram drafter (`Stockfish-PVS v2`) with `/dev/shm` KV slot snapshots (`13.1–32.6 ms` restore time for 40-tool Claude Code prompts) and an $O \left(\right. 1 \left.\right)$ speculative rollback fix for `deepseek4` recurrent/MLA states.

* * *

## Quantization & Memory Breakdown

To answer the most common technical question upfront—**exact bit-widths (`bpw`), base checkpoints, and what is compressed in each GGUF**:

| Checkpoint | Total / Active Params | Base Source | Disk Size (`GiB` / `GB`) | Effective `bpw` | Layer-by-Layer Tensor Allocation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **`Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Q4_0`** | `30.2B` / `3.0B` | BF16 Official | `17.59 GiB` (`18.89 GB`) | **`4.50 bpw`** | Standard `Q4_0` across MoE + attention; `F32` norms & SSM conv/decay |
| **`Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-MXFP4`** | `30.2B` / `3.0B` | BF16 Official | `15.95 GiB` (`17.13 GB`) | **`4.25 bpw`** | `GGML_TYPE_MXFP4` (`E2M1` + shared exponent) on routed MoE; `Q4_0`/`Q8_0` trunk |
| **`Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Fractal-64`** | `30.2B` / `3.0B` | BF16 Official | `14.35 GiB` (`15.41 GB`) | **`3.75 bpw`** | Attention, Mamba-2 SSM & shared experts in `Q4_0`/`Q8_0`/`F32`; cold routed MoE experts in hybrid `Q4_0` + `Fractal-64` (`Q2_0`, 64-weight block + `BF16` scale). Scores `100/100` on [`benchmarks/eval_quality_and_tools.py`](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip/blob/main/benchmarks/eval_quality_and_tools.py). |
| **`DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Fractal`** | `284.33B` / `13.17B` | Unsloth `UD-IQ1_S` (`76.87 GiB` / `82.5 GB`) | `56.56 GiB` (`60.73 GB`) | **`1.71 bpw`** | • **Embeddings, Dense L0, 43 Shared Experts (`shexp`), MLA `kv_a` / `q_a` / `wkv_b`:** Preserved in `Q4_K` / `Q5_K` / `F32` • **MLA `wq_b`&`attn_output` (`wo_a`/`wo_b`):** Transcoded to `Fractal-64` (`GGML_TYPE_Q2_0`, `3.75 bpw`, 30B/64-block w/ 8 sub-scales &`BF16` scale) • **256 Routed MoE Experts (`ffn_*_exps`):** Primarily `IQ1_S` (`1.5625 bpw`) with analytical `SwiGLU-H2` second-order scale matching; sensitive boundary layers preserved in `IQ2_XXS` (`2.06 bpw`) &`IQ1_M` (`1.75 bpw`) (`-20.31 GiB` vs `UD-IQ1_S`) |

> **Note on MoE Expert Routing (`Top-K`):** By default (`v2.4.0 Lossless`), `DeepSeek-V4-Flash` evaluates **all 6 routed experts + 1 shared expert (`Top-6`)** per layer with zero expert dropping (`1.00000` logit cosine similarity vs the unpatched runtime on the same checkpoint). Setting `LLAMA_MOE_TOP_K=5` or `4` is an optional runtime flag for users who want to trade a small perplexity delta for higher decode throughput.

* * *

## Quickstart

### Linux & macOS (Automated Setup & Chat)

git clone https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip.git
cd llama-modchip
./modchip chat

### Direct Run (Pre-Compiled Linux `x86_64` Binary + Hugging Face `.gguf`)

> **Compatibility Note (`GGML_TYPE_Q2_0 = 40`):**`Fractal-64` models use custom block-64 `BF16`-scale tensors (`GGML_TYPE_Q2_0`, type ID `40`) and `deepseek4` / `Stockfish-PVS` kernels. Unpatched `llama.cpp`, Ollama, or LM Studio binaries will reject them with `unknown tensor type 40`. Use `./modchip` above or the standalone pre-compiled binary (`llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64`, zero external `.so` dependencies) included in the Hugging Face repositories and [GitHub Release `v2.4.0`](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip/releases/tag/v2.4.0):

# 1. For 30B Nemotron-3.5-A3B (14.35 GiB — runs in 16–32 GB RAM at 25–60.4 tok/s):
hf download Synchopate/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Fractal-64-CPU-GGUF \
  llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64 NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Fractal-64.gguf --local-dir .
chmod +x llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64
./llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64 -m NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Fractal-64.gguf -c 262144 -t 16 --port 8080

# 2. For 284B DeepSeek-V4-Flash (56.56 GiB — fits in 64 GB RAM at 9.1–14.7 tok/s):
hf download Synchopate/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Fractal-64GB-CPU-GGUF --local-dir ./dsv4
chmod +x ./dsv4/llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64
./dsv4/llama-server-modchip-linux-x86_64 -m ./dsv4/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Fractal-00001-of-00003.gguf -c 32768 -t 16 -fa on --port 8080

### Windows 10/11 (Hybrid GPU + CPU MoE Pack)

Open **[`windows/`](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip/blob/main/windows/README.md)** and run **[`windows/AVVIA_MODCHIP.bat`](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip/blob/main/windows/AVVIA_MODCHIP.bat)** (or `./modchip start` in Git Bash). It detects physical CPU cores, free RAM, and GPU VRAM (`nvidia-smi`), downloads `llama.cpp` CUDA 12.4 / Vulkan binaries, computes the `--n-cpu-moe` split, and launches the Web Chat UI (`http://127.0.0.1:8080`).

| `./modchip` Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **`./modchip chat`** | Interactive terminal chat with live `tok/s`, TTFT, and `Stockfish-PVS` acceptance telemetry |
| **`./modchip web`** | Opens the Dark-Mode Web Chat & Live Telemetry HUD (`http://127.0.0.1:8787`) |
| **`./modchip bench`** | Runs a 30-second 2-stage speed test and prints a shareable CPU Benchmark Scorecard |
| **`./modchip claude`** | Launches Claude Code CLI (`40 tools`) wired to the local 256K engine (`18.9–32.6 ms` warm restore) |
| **`./modchip eval`** | Runs the reproducible 100-Point Quality, Tool-Calling, Coding & 8.5K Needle Gate |
| **`./modchip quantize`** | Transcodes `BF16`/`Q4_0`/`UD-IQ1_S` GGUFs into `Fractal-64` (`3.75 bpw`) or `Fractal-MXFP4` (`4.25 bpw`) |
| **`./modchip status` / `stop`** | Inspects CPU readiness, `2MB HugePages`, and `/dev/shm` IPC, or stops background services |

### Hardware Readiness Check (Zero Model Download Required)

curl -sL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/synchopate/llama-modchip/main/scripts/check_cpu_readiness.py | python3

Submit your terminal scorecard via a [GitHub Benchmark Issue](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip/issues/new?template=cpu_benchmark_submission.yml) or [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/synchopate/llama-modchip/discussions) to add your CPU to the leaderboard below.

Title: Outlook.com Is Quietly Rejecting Email From Domains Without DMARC

URL Source: https://mailroute.net/blog/outlook-rejecting-email-without-dmarc

Published Time: 2026-11-06

Markdown Content:
Since November 5, 2026, Microsoft's consumer mail service has been turning away some of the email from domains that don't publish a DMARC record. If your company emails customers, vendors or applicants with outlook.com, hotmail.com, live.com or msn.com addresses, some of that mail may be bouncing right now. Nobody announced it. The fix is one DNS record.

**Key takeaways**

*   Outlook.com, Hotmail, Live and MSN now refuse part of the mail from domains that have no DMARC record.
*   It hits ordinary, low-volume senders, not only the bulk senders Microsoft's published rules cover.
*   Only some messages bounce, so "my mail is getting through" doesn't mean your domain is safe.
*   The fix is a single TXT record, `v=DMARC1; p=none`, which changes nothing about how other receivers treat your mail.

## What the bounce looks like

The sender gets a bounce like this one, followed by a bracketed server name and ID that differ per message:

```
550 5.7.1 Message rejected: Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC Auth Records (AS9031519)
```

On the first day, the same rejection came back without the `(AS9031519)` code:

```
550 5.7.1 Message rejected: Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC Auth Records
```

The wording suggests something is badly broken. Usually it isn't. The domains we have seen bounced mostly had working SPF, and many had DKIM too. What they were missing was the DMARC record that ties the two to the From address.

## What changed

Microsoft does have published sender rules. Since May 2025, domains that send [more than 5,000 messages a day](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/microsoftdefenderforoffice365blog/strengthening-email-ecosystem-outlook%E2%80%99s-new-requirements-for-high%E2%80%90volume-senders/4399730) to Outlook.com have had to pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC, or get `550 5.7.515 Access denied`. That rule is aimed at marketers and bulk senders, and most small businesses rightly assumed it didn't apply to them.

This new rejection is different in the ways that matter:

*   **It reaches small senders.** A one-line reply from a small office can bounce.
*   **It wasn't announced.** As of November 6, Microsoft has published nothing about it: no postmaster notice, no blog post, no service-health entry.
*   **It doesn't say what failed.** A 5.7.515 bounce lists the SPF, DKIM and DMARC results. This one only says records are missing.

We first saw these bounces in our own outbound logs on November 5. Public reports from other administrators started appearing the same day.

## Why it's easy to miss

**Microsoft refuses only part of the mail** from an affected domain. One message to a Hotmail address goes through, the next one bounces, and a resend may succeed. That inconsistency is what makes this one dangerous: the person who sent the message sees a bounce full of acronyms, assumes a glitch, and moves on. The customer on the other end never knows a message was sent.

If your business depends on reaching people at personal addresses (patients, homeowners, applicants, parents, members), the cost is quiet. Invoices that don't arrive, appointment confirmations that never land, replies that look like you ignored someone.

## Is your domain affected?

Your domain is exposed if it has no DMARC record. You can check in a few seconds from any terminal. Replace `example.com` with your domain:

```
dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com
```

A line starting with `"v=DMARC1` means you have a record. No output means you don't. That's the case this rejection targets.

## The fix is one DNS record

Add a TXT record at your DNS host:

*   **Name:**`_dmarc`
*   **Value:**`v=DMARC1; p=none`

**`p=none` is the safe starting point.** It declares that your domain uses DMARC and asks receivers to send you reports, but it tells them to take no action on failures. Nothing about how Gmail, Yahoo or anyone else treats your mail changes.

There is one condition. DMARC passes only when SPF or DKIM passes _for the domain in your From address_. If neither lines up, a DMARC record alone won't help. We covered how alignment works, and why it's where most setups go wrong, in [SPF, DKIM, and DMARC Are No Longer Optional](https://mailroute.net/blog/email-authentication-now-mandatory).

Step-by-step instructions, including the checks for all three records, are in our [guide to the Outlook.com 5.7.1 error](https://mailroute.net/docs/admin/outlook-message-lacks-spf-dkim-dmarc-auth-records).

## If your mail goes through MailRoute

Mail you send through the MailRoute outbound relay already passes both checks DMARC needs:

*   **SPF.** Your mail keeps your own domain as its envelope sender and leaves from servers that [`include:spf.mailroute.net`](https://mailroute.net/docs/setup/implementing-spf-for-the-mailroute-outbound-smarthost-service) authorizes.
*   **DKIM.** We [sign every outbound message as your domain](https://mailroute.net/docs/setup/implementing-dkim-for-the-mailroute-outbound-smarthost-service), using the keys your `mr01`, `mr02` and `mr03` CNAME records point to. Publish all three, so we can rotate keys without your signatures ever breaking.

For MailRoute senders, the DMARC record is the whole fix. Once it's in place, Outlook.com sees a domain that authenticates, and DMARC passes on either check. Our guide to [publishing DMARC for the MailRoute outbound relay](https://mailroute.net/docs/setup/implementing-dmarc-for-the-mailroute-outbound-smarthost-service) takes you from `p=none` to enforcement when you're ready.

## If your mail doesn't go through MailRoute

The DMARC record is still the fix, but the service that sends your mail has to pass SPF or DKIM for your domain. Microsoft 365, for example, signs with its own `onmicrosoft.com` domain until you turn on DKIM for your own domain, and that signature doesn't count toward DMARC. Our sister company mxio has a [guide to this error for any sender](https://mxio.io/learn/errors/outlook-lacks-spf-dkim-dmarc-auth-records-5-7-1), with a checker that tests your domain from the page.

## Where this is heading

This is the pattern every major mailbox provider is following. Requirements start with the bulk senders, get announced with a deadline, and then quietly become the baseline for everyone. DMARC at `p=none` is the floor now, not a best practice.

That's not a bad thing. Spoofing is how much of today's phishing and business email compromise starts, and a domain that authenticates is a domain that's much harder to impersonate. The `p=none` record that gets your mail delivered to Outlook.com today is also the first step to `p=reject`, which tells receivers to refuse mail that forges your domain.

If you'd like a relay that signs your outbound mail correctly from day one, our [setup documentation](https://mailroute.net/docs/setup/set-up-spf-dkim-and-dmarc) walks through SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and you can [start a trial](https://mailroute.net/trial-request) whenever you're ready. Add the record today. It takes a few minutes, and it's one less reason for your mail to disappear.
