articles.title: Agent memory needs its OpenTelemetry moment
articles.content:
Title: Agent memory needs its OpenTelemetry moment — LoreKit blog

URL Source: https://www.lorekit.io/blog/open-agent-memory-format

Markdown Content:
## [Count the memory formats on your machine](https://www.lorekit.io/blog/open-agent-memory-format#count-the-memory-formats-on-your-machine)

List every place your coding tools keep something they "remember". A typical setup today:

*   an `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` in most repos, and `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` in a few
*   an agent writing files to a `/memories` directory through Anthropic's memory tool
*   Copilot keeping facts about each repo on GitHub's side
*   a memory MCP server keeping a JSONL knowledge graph

That's four different shapes, and **none of them can read the others**. A lesson your CI agent learns stays in whatever wrote it. Your editor agent can't read it, and neither can the next tool you try.

Each format is reasonable on its own. Together, they rebuild the same small idea again and again: _a note an agent left for its future self, stored at some address, true for a while._

And the list keeps growing. Browse r/ClaudeAI, r/LocalLLaMA or r/cursor and you'll find a steady stream of "I built a memory layer for my agent" posts, each with its own storage, its own schema and its own MCP tools. That's good evidence the problem is real: people keep hitting it badly enough to build something. But every new solution adds one more format that nothing else can read. **The problem isn't a missing tool. It's a missing agreement**, and that only comes from the community working on it together.

I build one of these tools, LoreKit, which is open source. This isn't a pitch that LoreKit has solved memory. Its format is one proposal among several, with gaps of its own. The point is that **this is the moment to agree on a shared shape**, and that another field has already shown how.

## [We've seen this before](https://www.lorekit.io/blog/open-agent-memory-format#weve-seen-this-before)

Before 2019, every observability vendor shipped its own agent, its own instrumentation library and its own data format. Switching vendors meant instrumenting your code again. Two open projects, OpenTracing and OpenCensus, tried to fix that and competed with each other too.

In 2019 they merged into **OpenTelemetry**. What mattered was what the vendors agreed to stop competing on:

1.   **A data model**: what a span, a metric and a log record are.
2.   **Semantic conventions**: shared names like `service.name` and `http.*`.
3.   **A protocol**: OTLP, one way to send the data.
4.   **Reference implementations**: shared SDKs and the Collector.

Vendors kept competing on what they _do_ with the data: storage, querying, analysis. Users instrument once. I work with OpenTelemetry every day at [Dash0](https://www.dash0.com/), and that agreement is why a whole ecosystem of tools can read each other's data.

The same four layers. Observability agreed on them and competes on what happens after the data arrives. Agent memory has plenty of implementations, but nothing agreed underneath them.

Agent memory is where observability was before 2019. The timing is good: the formats are young enough to change, and there's already a neutral home for agent standards. MCP and `AGENTS.md` both sit under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.

## [A tour of the shapes](https://www.lorekit.io/blog/open-agent-memory-format#a-tour-of-the-shapes)

These change quickly, so treat the details as a snapshot from late 2026.

| Family | Example | The unit of memory | Addressed by | Forgetting |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Instruction files | `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, Cursor `.mdc` rules | A whole Markdown file | File path (plus `globs` for Cursor) | Never. A person edits it |
| Agent-managed files | Anthropic's memory tool | A file under `/memories` | A path the model picks | Never, unless the model deletes it |
| Hosted repo facts | GitHub Copilot Memory | A fact with code citations | One repository | Deleted after 28 days unused |
| Context blocks | Letta core memory | A labeled block with a character `limit` | A `label` on an agent | Never. Always in context |
| Extracted facts | Mem0 | A fact the service extracts from messages | `user_id` / `agent_id` / `run_id` / `app_id` | Optional expiration date |
| Namespaced store | LangGraph `BaseStore` | A JSON `value` dict | A `namespace` tuple + `key` | Optional TTL, reset when the item is read (by default) |
| Knowledge graph | MCP reference memory server | Entities, relations, observations | Entity name | Never |
| Temporal graph | Graphiti / Zep | A fact on a graph edge | Entities + edge | Facts are invalidated rather than deleted, on two timelines |
| Addressed record | LoreKit | A record with a scope, key and lifecycle | A scope string + `key` | Never, unless a TTL is set |

A few of them got something right that a shared spec should keep. **Copilot Memory** pairs citations you can check against the code with forgetting by default, though it's locked inside one product. **LangGraph** shows how small the core can be: `put(namespace, key, value)`. **Graphiti** models time properly, with separate timelines for when a fact was true and when it was recorded. And **`AGENTS.md`** shows that a plain file at a known path can become a standard.

### [The proposals that already exist](https://www.lorekit.io/blog/open-agent-memory-format#the-proposals-that-already-exist)

Several people have started on this. MacPaw Research's **Portable Memory** is a `.mem` bundle with byte-reproducible serialization, deletion tombstones and optional signing; its authors say it isn't widely adopted yet. The **Open Memory Protocol** is an April 2026 draft for moving conversations and the memories derived from them between platforms as a ZIP with a manifest. Cognee's **COGX** format imports from Mem0, Letta and Zep.

These mostly solve **export**: moving one person's memory from vendor A to vendor B. Coding tools also have a second, open problem: **live addressing**. When a CI job, an editor agent and a review bot work in the same repo at once, how do they read and write the _same_ place and agree on what it means? A complete spec needs both.

Export moves one owner's memory between vendors. Live addressing lets many tools share one place at the same time. The existing proposals focus on the first. A shared address could sit inside their records to cover the second.

Strip away the branding and every format answers the same four questions differently: **where** a memory is true, **what its identity is** (does a second write update it or duplicate it?), **what it says**, and **when it stops being true**. Nobody disagrees that those matter. The tools only disagree on the answers, which is where OpenTelemetry started too.

There's one real fork: **who writes the memory**. In instruction files it's a person. In the memory tool, Letta and LoreKit, it's the model. In Mem0 and Graphiti, a service extracts facts from the conversation. A spec doesn't need to pick one. It needs to _record_ which, so a reader knows how much to trust what it reads.

Here's roughly what one record could look like as a file. It illustrates the data model; the field names aren't a proposal:

```
---
spec: agent-memory/0.1
id: 8f0c2a6e-4b1d-4c7a-9e2f-3a5b6c7d8e9f
address: { level: repo, value: github.com/acme/checkout }
key: tests-need-local-postgres
kind: lesson
written_by: { type: agent, name: claude-code }
content_type: text/markdown
lifecycle: { expires_at: null, extended_by: write }
attributes: { vcs.pr: 482, ci.run_url: "https://ci.example/runs/123" }
---
Integration tests fail with `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432` unless Postgres
is already running. Start it before `pnpm test`:

    docker compose up -d db

The test setup does not start it for you.
```

The frontmatter is the envelope: `address` and `key` say where it's true, `id` is its identity, `lifecycle` says when it stops, and `written_by` answers the fork. The Markdown below it is the memory itself, and `content_type` tells a reader how to treat it. Anything else a tool needs goes in `attributes`, under a namespace other tools can ignore. The same record serialises to JSON just as well, for a tool that wants to send it over the wire.

Around that record, a spec would mirror OpenTelemetry's layers:

*   **Conventions**: shared names for address levels (`global`, `project`, `repo`, `branch`, and whatever monorepos need), for kinds, and for attribute namespaces (`vcs.*`, `ci.*`, `agent.*`), in one versioned registry.
*   **A contract**: a few operations (write, read, list, search, archive) with fixed inputs and outputs, exposed over MCP. Many memory servers now offer an MCP interface, but each exposes different tools with different meanings.
*   **Conformance tests** in place of a reference implementation: round-trip a record and check nothing was lost, check that unknown attributes survive a rewrite, check that expiry behaves as stated.

What stays _out_ matters as much: storage, ranking, embeddings, the user interface. That's where tools should compete. And the spec should live somewhere neutral, not in LoreKit's repo or any single vendor's.

## [What a skeptic would say](https://www.lorekit.io/blog/open-agent-memory-format#what-a-skeptic-would-say)

**"You build a memory tool, so of course you want a standard shaped like it."** Fair. It's why LoreKit is one row in the table rather than the template. If a shared spec looks different, LoreKit should adopt it anyway.

**"MCP already is the standard."** MCP standardises the _call_, not the _record_. OpenTelemetry needed a protocol _and_ a data model. Memory needs both too.

**"Shared memory is a prompt-injection channel."** Yes. Anything an agent reads can steer it, and shared memory widens who gets to write it. A spec should make that visible: record who wrote each memory, allow signatures (Portable Memory already does), and let a record point at the code it depends on so a reader can check whether that code changed. No format makes poisoning impossible.

**"Another standard won't fix fragmentation."** That's [xkcd 927](https://xkcd.com/927/), and it's the strongest objection. My answer is OpenTelemetry's: agreement came when existing projects _merged_, not when someone added another one. The work here is the same: take what the existing proposals and tools each got right, and agree on the parts they share.

## [Open questions](https://www.lorekit.io/blog/open-agent-memory-format#open-questions)

I don't know the answers to these, and I'd rather work them out in public:

*   **Which address levels?** Monorepos want a level between `repo` and `branch`. Should levels be a fixed list or conventions?
*   **Should forgetting be the default?** Copilot forgets by default, LoreKit doesn't, and LangGraph extends life on read.
*   **Should a record point at the code it depends on?** It's the best protection against stale memory, but it ties a record to a code host.
*   **Who should coordinate?** A working group, a foundation, or a draft spec people send changes to?

If you build any of the tools in the table, or wrote one of the proposals, I'd like to compare notes. LoreKit's schema and on-disk format are MIT-licensed as one concrete input. To see real records, LoreKit's offline store writes plain Markdown files you can open, grep and diff:

`npx @lorekit/cli install`
Compare them with what your other tools write, and tell me what a shared format would need that none of them have yet.

articles.title: How I Fight AI Brain Fry
articles.content:
Title: How I'm fighting the AI Brain Fry — Sergey Kuhne

URL Source: https://sergeykuhne.com/blog/fighting-ai-brain-fry

Markdown Content:
If you work with Claude Code or Codex from the terminal, you know this one.

You start a task. The AI takes time to reply, so you start another one. Then the first one replies, but the reply needs one clarification, one follow up and one side task — and each of them wants its own tab. Then the second tab's reply comes in. You juggle. And all of a sudden you find yourself hopping between 20 threads, trying to keep all those contexts in your brain RAM.

Until you can't. Your brain gets exhausted, your focus smashes, and you don't know anymore what you were doing, where you started, and where you were supposed to finish.

A lot of people are suggesting taking breaks, thinking before typing, limiting scope. I have my own experiment.

I decided this way of working has two major problems: sequencing and context. So I organised my work a bit like a priority queue.

Here is how it actually works.

The queue lives in git. Every ticket is a markdown file in the repo, right next to the code it talks about, and the state of the board is a committed snapshot. Nothing important lives in a chat window and nothing lives in my head. If a session dies, the queue is still there.

An agent works that board in cycles. It researches new tickets, builds the ones a human has tagged as safe to build, runs the tests and a browser check, and verifies what is already deployed. For anything touching sensitive code it builds on a branch and asks first. It never deploys to production — that part is mine.

What it cannot do is decide. So everything that needs me lands in one place I call my owner inbox. A script reads the whole board and hands me a prioritised list of exactly the items waiting on my judgement — review this change, answer this question, rule on this tradeoff.

The reading surface is a Claude artifact. One page, rebuilt from git on every cycle, mirroring the whole board plus a review page per ticket. So I don't scroll back through a terminal trying to reconstruct what a change does. I open one link, read what was built and why, and give my verdict. The verdict goes back into git, onto the card. The page is only a viewer — git is the record.

Then comes the part that matters most.

I take one item. I load its context. I make a decision or request an action. And I close it, by putting it back into the queue.

That closing is the whole trick. The ticket doesn't keep hanging in my memory as a thing to remember about. The context closes with it. So when I pick the next item from the queue, I can actually focus. One thing at a time.

It is still exhausting. But I don't feel distracted or lost.

The challenge was, and still is, the tooling around it. Getting the context served up in a digestible manner, so loading a ticket takes a minute and not twenty. And keeping tickets from going into endless loops because they are blocked waiting for a ruling only I can give.

It's a living organism and I keep improving it. But it felt like a huge step forward in my productivity with AI tools, so I thought it was worth sharing.

articles.title: I'm not a fan of Deno's security model (2024)
articles.content:
Title: I’m not a fan of Deno’s security model

URL Source: https://goldstein.lol/posts/deno-security/

Markdown Content:
(published on August 31, 2024)
this has been bothering me for a while now, so I want to write down my thoughts so I can get it out of my head and move on. we’re gonna talk about how Deno approaches security, specifically with its permissions system, and why I think this approach is fundamentally insecure and misleading.

## [wait, what’s Deno?](https://goldstein.lol/posts/deno-security/#wait-whats-deno)
[Deno](https://deno.com/) is a language runtime for JavaScript. it consists of a standard library, a package manager, a TypeScript transpiler and a bunch of other stuff that’s not important for our story. it’s not a JavaScript _implementation_, so it does not interpret or compile JavaScript, it reuses V8 for that.

one of the flagship features of Deno is its permission system (it’s under the “Secure by default” header on their [landing page](https://deno.com/)). the idea is simple: as JS code running in Deno needs the standard library to access the outside world, Deno can choose which accesses it allows or disallows, so when you run

shell`deno run --allow-read=/tmp/dir --allow-run=uname code.ts`

the standard library will only allow `code.ts` to read `/tmp/dir` and run `uname`.

additionally, a program can request permissions at runtime, so code like

typescript
```
const r = { name: "read", path: "/tmp/dir" } as const;
await Deno.permissions.request(r);
```

will display a nice little prompt in the terminal:

```
┌ ⚠️  Deno requests read access to "/tmp/dir".
├ Requested by `Deno.permissions.request()` API.
├ Run again with --allow-read to bypass this prompt.
└ Allow? [y/n/A] (y = yes, allow; n = no, deny; A = allow all read permissions) >
```

and you can grant or refuse it.

(aside: I really miss this feature in browser extensions. currently, if your extension needs _potential_ access to _any_ website, it needs to request _actual_ access to _all_ the websites, which is less than ideal)

if you like puzzles, this is the point where you can stop and think about what could go wrong with this system.

## [the prompts problem](https://goldstein.lol/posts/deno-security/#the-prompts-problem)
of the two specific issues I want to point out this is the less severe one. we’ll discuss it first because this was the first thing I noticed and it kinda immediately irked me when I first read about this.

(if you’re only interested in the more juicy part, you can skip to the [next section](https://goldstein.lol/posts/deno-security/#the---allow-run-problem)).

so, this nice little prompt is displayed in the terminal. it’s not, like, a PolKit GUI window or anything, it’s just text on stdout waiting for input from stdin. this is a wild thing to do.

you see, terminal has a somewhat weird API. most of the commands / requests application can send to the terminal are sent in-band, by printing them to stdout. terminal can then reply by sending data to stdin. as Deno allows programs to print arbitrary data to stdout and read from stdin without requiring any permissions or doing any filtering, malicious code can send arbitrary commands to the terminal. it’s usually okay, because terminals won’t, like, execute shell commands just because stdout told them to, you’re supposed to be able to freely `cat` files without risking arbitrary code execution. it’s markedly less okay if you allow malicious code to do whatever with the terminal and then print a prompt on the same exact terminal.

you could, like, [hide the prompt by messing with terminal colors](https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/9666). (this one got closed in 2026 because the permission prompt is “partially visible” (you can see an emoji) and “AI agents tend to” change terminal colors, so that’s a “valid use-case”)

or [trick the user into pre-feeding approval into stdin](https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/9750).

or [trick the terminal into feeding approval into stdin as a response to some request](https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/9750#issuecomment-796702901). (terminal won’t ever send Enter to stdin to avoid executing commands, but “press Enter to continue” is common enough to not be suspicious; the user never sees the actual prompt). here’s [an asciicast of that](https://asciinema.org/a/9rvK8ANJK0WnQc9nsrFKdC7ir), I think it looks quite cool.

the specific issue on the screencast is long patched; the issue with terminal colors is not. that doesn’t really matter because the _real_ issue is using an attacker-controlled channel for security-sensitive information. it’s like executing attacker-controlled JS code on a webpage and then asking for password on the same page. you can’t know that the page is in a safe state, so you can’t trust any input.

even if Deno manages to patch every single issue with the “standard” escape codes, you never know which non-standard codes even exist out there. many terminals have some, it’s impossible to predict how they will interact with your prompt.

(aside: how come sudo can do it then? the difference is that sudo asks for the password first, before running any other code. to trick sudo that way you’d need to fuck up terminal state before you even type `sudo`, and do it quietly enough that you don’t notice it while you type it. if some terminal allows it, I’d consider it a bug in the terminal)

## [the `--allow-run` problem](https://goldstein.lol/posts/deno-security/#the---allow-run-problem)
so, there’s a weird thing with this command I wrote above (I’ll copy it here for reference):

shell`deno run --allow-read=/tmp/dir --allow-run=uname code.ts`

what does `--allow-run=uname` even mean? it’s not like programs have canonical names, it’s not `org.gnu.coreutils.uname`, it’s not even `/nix/store/8k1dmzr3gwzqdgw45nzj76902ca7g1is-coreutils-full-9.5/bin/uname`. it’s just a shortcut for “look at all the directories in `PATH` one-by-one to see if you can find `uname` there”.

you can set environment variables for the child process without needing any extra permissions, so what if we just

```
$ cat t.ts
const command = new Deno.Command("uname", {
  // my current working directory, can be anything
  env: { 'PATH': '/tmp/tmp.7ofmKaNW83' },
});
const { code, stdout, stderr } = command.outputSync();
console.log(new TextDecoder().decode(stdout));
$ cat uname
#!/bin/sh
printf lol
$ deno run --allow-run=uname t.ts
lol
```

yeah.

once again, we have a pretty and convenient interface that doesn’t really make sense from the security standpoint. it would be _nice_ if programs were uniquely identified by their names, but they’re _not_, and pretending they are leads to security holes.

funnily enough, I didn’t even think that this issue would be there when I poked at Deno for the first time, so I haven’t reported it [until now](https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/11964#issuecomment-2322993158) (spoiler alert: this is a comment on a GitHub issue that I created for the problem I’ll explain below).

so let’s imagine we fixed that. it’s not _that_ hard, we can force `PATH` to be whatever it was when the runtime started, or always require fully-qualified paths, or prompt with a fully-qualified path before running. are we safe now?

lol no of course we’re not. while `PATH` decides which executable gets run, dynamically-linked executables (so, like, most executables) require dynamic loader to actually start. dynamic loader is a program that, well, loads the executable into memory, finds its dependencies and does a bunch of other fun stuff we won’t get into. the important part is that dynamic loader is _configurable_ via environment variables. you can probably see where this is going now.

`LD_PRELOAD` instructs the dynamic loader to load specific dynamic library when loading executables. dynamic libraries can execute arbitrary code on load. we can just pass `LD_PRELOAD` and we’ve completely escaped the sandbox once again:

```
$ cat t.c
#include <stdio.h>

// ask dynamic loader to run this function on load time pretty please
__attribute__((constructor)) void lol() {
    puts("lol");
}
$ cat t.ts
const command = new Deno.Command("uname", {
  // ask dynamic loader to load our evil library
```

I [reported this](https://github.com/denoland/deno/issues/11964) some time ago and now they [patched it](https://github.com/denoland/deno/pull/25271) by disallowing to set environment variables starting with `LD_`. this, once again, fixes a specific issue while ignoring the larger problem: “permission to run a single command” is mostly not a useful concept. (you _can_ do secure interfaces by allowing to run a single command, like git-over-SSH does, but generally both the environment and the command need to be prepared to handle it)

say, for example, our script wants to invoke the `$EDITOR` so user can edit some data (think git commit messages). that’s a very natural permission request, and it’s also an unmitigated disaster because most editors are configurable enough for running one to be a full sandbox escape. it’s easy for user to absent-mindedly grant `--allow-run=vim` (“well, sure, I want to edit this file!”), but then the script can just set `VIMINIT='!rm -rf /*'` and oops, all my files are gone. most programs are configurable, often in some ways you won’t think about (like `LD_PRELOAD`), and attacker controls the execution enviornment. “patch some specific ways to configure programs” is not the solution, the solution is to sandbox all the code, not just JS code.

when we discussed all this stuff in GitHub issues, a Deno developer wrote:

> The main thing it protects you against is malicious code that isn't smart enough.

upon reading this, I was enlightened.

## [conclusions](https://goldstein.lol/posts/deno-security/#conclusions)
deno tries really hard to do what the operating system should be doing. it emulates syscall filtering by filtering standard library calls. unfortunately, this breaks down the second you need to run code that doesn’t use Deno standard library. it also uses somewhat flawed approach to permission management that _looks_ good (wow, runtime prompts! omg, I can just `--allow-run=uname`!), but introduces security risks. in doing this, it implicitly requires user to understand all the implications of various permissions and their combinations, which can be really hard.

Deno process is not actually sandboxed, it only pretends it is. I didn’t mention some more boring issues like “Deno doesn’t prevent you from following symlinks that lead outside of the sandbox” because they all just boil down to this simple one: the process is not sandboxed.

one can argue that this pseudo-sandboxing is better than nothing: after all, not all the malicious code is smart enough. I disagree: Deno permissions give a false sense of security and can lure someone into running untrusted code without proper sandboxing.

it’s possible that you can use Deno sandboxing safely if you:

*   never use more dangerous permissions like `--allow-run`, even with `=cmd`,
*   that includes `--allow-env`, even `--allow-env=VAR`, for setting environment variables is memory unsafe and can affect libc functions,
*   preferrably run with `--no-prompt` so your terminal can’t be tricked,
*   are careful about symlinks in directories you `--allow-{read,write}` to,
*   are not concerned with resource exhaustion: there’re zero permissions required to burn CPU or allocate memory.

in particular, you may be safe if you’re running untrusted code with no permissions at all in a non-interactive context and use some other mechanism to control resource consumption.
